concepts.name: IFC's Institutional Identity and World Bank Group Membership
key_dimensions: IFC as a distinct legal entity vs. its position as one of five World Bank Group institutions
Distinction from IBRD and IDA — IFC exclusively targets private sector, not governments
Year of establishment (1956) and founding rationale — filling the gap IBRD left for private enterprise
UPSC trap: Confusing IFC with IDA (both deal with developing countries but IDA lends to governments, IFC to private sector)

concepts.name: IFC's Core Mandate and Developmental Mission
key_dimensions: Primary mandate: Furthering economic development by encouraging private sector growth in developing countries
Dual objective — development impact AND financial sustainability (profit-making body unlike IDA)
Focus on emerging markets and frontier economies where private capital is scarce
Distinction from purely commercial banks: development additionality as a prerequisite for investment

concepts.name: IFC Membership Structure and Voting Rights
key_dimensions: Membership conditionality: A country must be a member of IBRD to join IFC
Current membership count (~185 members) and significance of near-universal membership
Voting power structure: Shares held proportional to economic size, unlike UN's one-country-one-vote
UPSC trap: IFC membership is NOT the same as World Bank membership — IBRD membership is the gateway

concepts.name: IFC's Financial Instruments and Investment Portfolio
key_dimensions: Equity investments, loans, quasi-equity, guarantees, and risk management products — breadth of instruments
IFC does NOT require government guarantees (key differentiator from IBRD/IDA)
Syndicated loans and mobilization of private capital alongside IFC's own investment
UPSC trap: IFC can take equity stakes — it is a shareholder in private companies, not just a lender

concepts.name: IFC vs. MIGA vs. IBRD vs. IDA — Comparative Roles within World Bank Group
key_dimensions: IBRD: Loans to middle-income and creditworthy low-income governments
IDA: Concessional loans and grants to poorest governments
IFC: Loans and equity to private sector in developing countries
MIGA: Political risk insurance and guarantees for private investors; ICSID: dispute resolution — complete five-body map

concepts.name: IFC's Governance Structure: Board of Governors and Board of Directors
key_dimensions: Board of Governors — highest authority, one governor per member country (typically Finance Minister/Central Bank Governor)
Board of Directors — 25 Executive Directors, handles day-to-day policy; shared with World Bank Group but IFC has separate board
President of IFC: Same as World Bank Group President (currently Ajay Banga) — shared leadership structure
UPSC trap: IFC has its own President (who is the World Bank Group President) but separate Articles of Agreement

concepts.name: IFC's Articles of Agreement — Key Provisions and Prohibitions
key_dimensions: Article I: Purposes — private sector development without displacing private capital (additionality principle)
Prohibition on financing projects where adequate private capital is available on reasonable terms
IFC cannot accept government guarantees — enshrined in Articles, not just policy
Political non-interference clause: IFC decisions must be based on economic considerations alone

concepts.name: IFC's Environmental and Social Performance Standards
key_dimensions: Eight Performance Standards (PS) covering areas: environmental assessment, labor, biodiversity, indigenous peoples, etc.
IFC Performance Standards have become the global benchmark adopted by Equator Principles banks
Equator Principles: Voluntary framework adopted by 130+ private financial institutions based on IFC standards
UPSC relevance: IFC standards influence private lending globally — their extraterritorial regulatory significance

concepts.name: The Equator Principles and IFC's Standard-Setting Role
key_dimensions: Equator Principles (EPs) launched in 2003, revised multiple times, currently EP4 (2020)
Apply to project finance above $10 million threshold in emerging markets AND developed countries
IFC Performance Standards are the reference framework — IFC is the de facto global regulator for project finance ESG
UPSC trap: Equator Principles are voluntary, NOT legally binding — adopted by private banks independently

concepts.name: IFC's Role in India — Historical and Strategic Investments
key_dimensions: India among IFC's largest client countries; investments in infrastructure, financial sector, manufacturing, agribusiness
IFC's India investments: renewable energy, affordable housing, MSME financing, healthcare
IFC issued India's first green bond (Masala Bond in rupees on London Stock Exchange, 2013) — landmark event
IFC's partnership with SIDBI, NABARD, and private NBFCs for on-lending to MSMEs

concepts.name: Masala Bonds and IFC's Capital Market Innovations
key_dimensions: IFC issued the first Masala Bond in 2013 — rupee-denominated bond sold to foreign investors, currency risk borne by investor
Significance: Internationalizing Indian Rupee, developing offshore rupee bond market
Distinction from External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs): In ECBs, Indian borrower bears currency risk; in Masala Bonds, investor bears risk
IFC's broader role in developing local currency bond markets across emerging economies

concepts.name: IFC's Additionality Principle
key_dimensions: Core test for IFC investment: Would the project proceed without IFC on acceptable terms? If yes, IFC should not invest
Three types of additionality: Financial additionality, knowledge/advisory additionality, and demonstration/catalytic effect
Additionality distinguishes IFC from a commercial bank — it must crowd in private capital, not crowd it out
UPSC trap: IFC being profit-making does NOT make it purely commercial; additionality requirement is the key constraint

concepts.name: IFC's Advisory Services and Technical Assistance
key_dimensions: IFC provides advisory services separately from investment — helping businesses and governments improve investment climate
Areas: Corporate governance, PPP advisory, business environment reform, SME capacity building
Funded partly through donor contributions and IFC's own income — not from investment returns alone
Distinction: Advisory arm helps create the enabling environment; investment arm deploys capital — two complementary pillars

concepts.name: IFC's Funding Mechanisms and Financial Sustainability
key_dimensions: IFC raises funds from international capital markets by issuing bonds (AAA-rated) — NOT primarily from member subscriptions
IFC's AAA credit rating allows it to borrow cheaply and on-lend at competitive rates
IFC retains earnings and builds reserves — does NOT distribute dividends to shareholders (unlike commercial entities)
UPSC trap: IFC does NOT rely on member government appropriations like IDA does — it is financially self-sustaining

concepts.name: IFC's Sector Priorities: Infrastructure, Financial Markets, and Climate Finance
key_dimensions: Infrastructure: Power, transport, water — IFC often acts as anchor investor to attract private capital
Financial markets: Lending to banks and MFIs for on-lending to MSMEs and underserved segments
Climate finance: IFC committed to align all investments with Paris Agreement; target of 35% of own-account investments in climate
IFC's 2030 targets under Creating Markets approach — systematic market creation in frontier/IDA countries

concepts.name: IFC's Creating Markets Approach and Upstream Work
key_dimensions: Upstream work: IFC works with governments to improve regulations and create investable projects before investing
Distinct from traditional downstream investment approach — addresses market failures at policy level
Focus on IDA countries and Fragile and Conflict-affected Situations (FCS) where normal markets fail
UPSC relevance: IFC's role in public-private partnership structuring and enabling regulatory environments

concepts.name: IFC and the Cascade Approach
key_dimensions: Cascade principle: First use private finance, if insufficient use guarantees/de-risking, only as last resort use public/concessional finance
Adopted by World Bank Group post-2017 to maximize private sector mobilization
IFC is central to Cascade — it represents the private finance and de-risking layers
UPSC trap: Cascade does NOT mean IDA/IBRD is being phased out — it means private finance is prioritized where feasible

concepts.name: IFC's Role in Green and Sustainable Finance
key_dimensions: IFC launched Green Bond Principles and has been a pioneer in green bond issuance since 2010
IFC's EDGE (Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies) — green building certification system used in 170+ countries
Climate finance commitments: IFC tracks climate-related investments using its own methodology aligned with MDB harmonization
Distinction: IFC green bonds finance private sector projects; World Bank green bonds finance government projects

concepts.name: IFC's Compliance Advisor Ombudsman (CAO)
key_dimensions: CAO is the independent accountability mechanism for IFC (and MIGA) — handles complaints from project-affected communities
Three functions: Ombudsman (dispute resolution), Compliance (audit of IFC's adherence to policies), Advisory
CAO is independent of IFC management — reports directly to World Bank Group President
UPSC trap: CAO covers IFC and MIGA only, NOT IBRD/IDA (which have their own Inspection Panel)

concepts.name: IFC's Differential Treatment of Developed vs. Developing Country Investments
key_dimensions: IFC primarily invests in developing and emerging market countries — not in high-income OECD countries
Frontier strategy: Increased focus on IDA-eligible countries, LDCs, and Sub-Saharan Africa
Country eligibility criteria differ from IBRD's — IFC uses per capita income thresholds and private sector need
UPSC relevance: India's graduation from IDA to IBRD-only country and implications for IFC's India strategy
